items.q: An attic perforation with foul discharge and white keratin debris indicates what?
items.exp: Attic or marginal perforations harbour cholesteatoma: keratinising epithelium eroding bone with foul pseudomonal discharge. It mandates surgical removal, unlike safe central disease.
r: Incorrect. Safe disease uses central perforations.
Correct. Attic keratin disease is cholesteatoma.
Incorrect. Glue ear has intact drum without discharge.
Incorrect. Canal disease spares attic drum lesions.
items.kp: Attic hole plus foul keratin: unsafe ear.

items.q: Cholesteatoma is best defined histologically as what?
o: Keratinising squamous epithelium in middle ear trapping keratin
items.exp: Despite its name, cholesteatoma is misplaced keratinising skin (not tumour, not cholesterol) accumulating keratin that expands and erodes bone. Cholesterol granuloma is a separate bloody middle ear lesion.
r: Incorrect. It is benign misplaced epithelium, not malignancy.
Correct. Skin in middle ear trapping keratin.
Incorrect. Cholesterol granuloma differs histologically.
Incorrect. Wax sits in canal and removes easily.
items.kp: Not cancer, not cholesterol: trapped skin keratin.

items.q: Definitive treatment of cholesteatoma is what?
items.exp: Only surgery excises cholesteatoma matrix and diseased mastoid, creating safe ear; drops and antibiotics merely reduce discharge temporarily. Delay risks intracranial spread.
r: Incorrect. Drops temporise discharge only.
Correct. Mastoid surgery is definitive.
Incorrect. Antibiotics cannot remove keratin matrix.
Incorrect. Syringing spreads infection through perforation.
items.kp: Keratin sacs come out surgically or not at all.

items.q: Chronic ear discharge with new vertigo suggests which complication?
items.exp: Cholesteatoma eroding the lateral semicircular canal fistulises the labyrinth, causing pressure induced vertigo, or infects it as labyrinthitis with deafness. This needs urgent ENT care.
r: Incorrect. Wax causes canal blockage, not fistula vertigo.
Correct. Erosion into labyrinth causes vertigo.
Incorrect. Effusion deafens without acute vertigo.
Incorrect. Otosclerosis fixes stapes without discharge.
items.kp: Chronic ear plus spinning: labyrinth breached.

items.q: Safe CSOM perforation is characteristically located where?
items.exp: Central pars tensa perforations with mucosal disease define safe tubotympanic CSOM. Attic (flaccida) and marginal perforations signal cholesteatoma risk and unsafe disease.
r: Incorrect. Attic perforation is unsafe cholesteatoma site.
Correct. Central pars tensa means safe disease.
Incorrect. Marginal perforations are unsafe.
Incorrect. Intact drum excludes discharging CSOM.
items.kp: Centre is safe; edges and attic are dangerous.

items.q: Most acquired cholesteatomas arise by which mechanism?
o: Retraction pocket from Eustachian dysfunction trapping keratin
items.exp: Chronic negative middle ear pressure retracts the attic drum into a self trapping pocket whose keratin cannot clear, expanding as cholesteatoma. Other routes (migration, metaplasia) are less common.
r: Incorrect. Cholesteatoma grows locally, not haematogenous.
Correct. Retraction pocket trapping keratin.
Incorrect. No viral oncogenesis involved.
Incorrect. Implantation after trauma is rare minority route.
items.kp: Sucked in attic pocket that cannot self clean.

items.q: Canal wall down mastoidectomy trades anatomy for what advantage?
o: Exteriorised disease visible for surveillance and cleaning
items.exp: Opening mastoid into canal exteriorises residual disease for direct inspection and cleaning, reducing hidden recurrence, at cost of lifelong cavity maintenance and water precautions.
r: Incorrect. Cavities need regular lifelong care.
Correct. Visible exteriorised cavity aids surveillance.
Incorrect. Hearing often worse than wall up reconstructions.
Incorrect. Cavity care is the main burden.
items.kp: Wall down: watch it easily, clean it forever.

items.q: Congenital cholesteatoma is recognised by what presentation?
o: White mass behind intact drum in a child
items.exp: Embryonic epithelial rests grow as white pearls behind intact drums in children without infection history, found on routine otoscopy. Acquired disease needs perforation or retraction history.
r: Incorrect. That is acquired attic disease.
Correct. Intact drum white mass in child.
Incorrect. Discharge implies acquired infected disease.
Incorrect. Trauma gives perforation, not congenital pearl.
items.kp: Quiet white pearl behind whole drum in child: congenital.

items.q: A dry central perforation with conductive loss is best offered what?
items.exp: Dry safe perforations are closed by myringoplasty grafting, restoring drum barrier and often hearing. Mastoidectomy is for cholesteatoma or refractory mastoid disease; drops treat only wet flares.
r: Incorrect. No mastoid disease to remove in dry safe ear.
Correct. Graft the dry central hole.
Incorrect. Aids help but surgery offered first where suitable.
Incorrect. Drops do not close perforations.
items.kp: Dry central hole: graft it closed.

items.q: Imaging best detecting residual cholesteatoma after surgery is what?
items.exp: Non echo planar diffusion MRI highlights keratin pearls brightly, detecting residual or recurrent cholesteatoma without second look surgery. CT shows bone anatomy but cannot distinguish pearl from scar reliably.
r: Incorrect. Plain films lack sensitivity.
Correct. Diffusion MRI finds keratin pearls.
Incorrect. CT cannot separate pearl from granulation.
Incorrect. Ultrasound cannot image mastoid bone disease.
items.kp: After surgery, diffusion MRI hunts leftover pearls.
